title: Latency-constrained tool schematic and SDK handoff notes
content:
Context: quick brain-dump / early PRD for how the Hosted API should behave when tool-calls / structured outputs are used in latency-sensitive paths (mobile micro-interactions, critical user flows). Not prescriptive yet; meant to capture constraints, developer ergonomics, and a pragmatic rollout plan.

Problem statement:
- Customers building fast UX (autocomplete, snippet generation, inline assistant) need tool-calling and structured outputs but cannot afford >150ms additional tail latency for small requests.
- Current streaming + tool-handshake designs assume a relaxed budget; SDKs and clients end up blocking or doing heavyweight reconciliation when network conditions or backpressure occur.
- We lack a compact, well-defined fallback semantics for partial/failed tool resolution that SDKs can implement offline with minimal developer overhead.

Success metrics (early):
- P99 end-to-end additional latency attributable to tool-handshake <= 120ms for 80% of small (<=64-token) requests on mobile profiles.
- SDK integration time for a basic tool set (search + action) < 2 dev hours using playbook/sample.
- Fallback correctness (no user-visible crashes) for 99.9% of tool failures in staged experiments.

Users & personas:
- Mobile app developer integrating hosted streaming assistant (needs lightweight SDKs).
- Product engineer for web editor requiring deterministic structured responses and graceful degradation.
- Platform integrator evaluating Hosted API for low-latency microfeatures.

Non-goals:
- Not solving full transactional tool orchestrations (we defer complex multi-tool sagas to Dedicated patterns).
- Not designing the final schema language for every use-case (we’ll define a minimal canonical structure and iterative extensions).

Constraints and assumptions:
- We assume typical mobile RTTs 40–120ms; server-side processing under our control must be smaller than client-side variability.
- SDKs can be updated frequently (semver compatibility required) but many customers will be pinned to older minor versions for weeks.
- We must support both streaming (incremental tokens) and batch responses (single JSON result) with consistent fallback behavior.

Design principles:
1) Make the common case cheap: prefer fast-paths that avoid synchronous external tool handoffs when time-budget is tight.
2) Prefer explicit, small schemas for tool intents so SDKs can pre-declare fallback templates without parsing heavy output.
3) Make degradation explicit: a response can include graded fidelity markers developers can surface in the UI.
4) Observability-first: SDKs should emit events for handshake start/finish, fallback triggered, and final resolution.

API / Protocol sketches (high level):
- Request envelope fields (client -> hosted API):
  - prompt, max_tokens, streaming: boolean, latency_budget_ms: optional int, tool_policies: list of tool descriptors (id, required|preferred)
- Response incremental frames (server -> client streaming):
  - FRAME types: TEXT, STRUCTURED, TOOL_HANDSHAKE_START, TOOL_HANDSHAKE_PROGRESS, TOOL_HANDSHAKE_RESULT, FIDELITY_HINT
- Key idea: latency_budget_ms is a soft SLO the runtime uses to decide: 1) whether to inline tool-call and wait; 2) whether to speculate a cached/approx result; 3) whether to skip tool invocation and emit a fallback placeholder.

Example fast-path handshake flow (<=150ms budget):
1) Client sends streaming request with latency_budget_ms=120.
2) Model emits early tokens and signals a required tool call (TOOL_HANDSHAKE_START frame).
3) Runtime checks availability/coldness of tool and typical tool latency. If estimated tool latency + expected token emission > budget -> runtime emits TOOL_HANDSHAKE_RESULT with \"fallback:template_id=search_stub_v1\" and continues streaming model tokens with a FIDELITY_HINT indicating partial results.
4) SDK receives fallback template id and can immediately render a lightweight placeholder UI (e.g., \"Searching…\" component becomes a predicted card using template).
5) If tool later completes, server sends TOOL_HANDSHAKE_RESULT with final data and a replayable patch frame that SDK can apply (atomic patch semantics).

SDK ergonomics (developer-facing):
- Minimal integration points: 
  - onPartialFrame(frame) -> developers get structured frames (typed).
  - onToolStub(templateId) -> UI can mount placeholder widget; library includes small template library for common tool types (search result list, URL-link, code-run output).
  - applyPatch(patchFrame) -> SDK attempts to merge deterministic patches into the displayed UI.
- Default behavior (if app developer does nothing): SDK auto-renders a simple placeholder and replaces it on final patch. This protects shipping fast.
- Opt-in stronger behavior: SDK exposes small adapter hooks where developers can supply custom rendering and reconciliation logic.

Structured output and schema negotiation:
- Provide a canonical minimal tool result envelope: {"type":"tool_result","tool_id":"search","schema_version":"1","payload":<opaque JSON>}.
- Schema negotiation: clients can send accepted_schema_versions per tool; runtime will attempt to normalize older tool responses into accepted versions when possible and mark normalization frames.
- For streaming partial structured outputs, we support incremental JSONL-like frames but enforce small, typed deltas rather than full re-sends to keep bandwidth low.

Fallback levels (explicit values):
- FULL: tool completed, final data present.
- PARTIAL: partial/approximate data (ranking with trimmed fields).
- STUB: template-only response (no real tool call performed).
- OMIT: tool intentionally skipped; model summary only.

Observability & telemetry requirements:
- SDK emits events: handshake_start, handshake_decision(fallback|inline|speculated|deferred), handshake_result(level), patch_applied(success|conflict), fallback_rendered.
- Server-side logs: record decision rationale (estimated_tool_latency, budget_ms, cache_hit boolean, route_id) to debug false fallbacks.
- Per-route dashboards: P95 rollback patch size, frequency of stubs, average time-to-final for patched results.

Edge cases and reconciliation:
- Patch conflicts: final tool result may contradict speculative model output. SDK patch application should be atomic and provide a simple diff event so apps can choose whether to replace, merge, or nudge user.
- Client offline scenario: if final patch cannot be delivered, SDK should surface an unobtrusive state (\"finalizing — connect to get full results\"). Server should mark the session with a replay token so a reconnect can request pending patches.

Rollout plan (staged):
1) Internal dogfood with console + one low-risk partner -> collect telemetry for handshake decisions and user-visible regressions.
2) Beta SDK (web + mobile) behind feature flag; provide quickstart with two sample adapters (search + run-code).
3) Gradual default enable for low-latency routes only; provide opt-out via route config.
4) Post-rollout: iterate on template library and expand schema normalization.

Safety & privacy notes:
- Tool stubs MUST include explicit markers for downstream privacy scanners; avoid accidental exposure of tool-intent or tool payloads in logs without redaction controls.
- Customer-configurable flags to disable speculation or stubbing for regulated customers.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the exact wire format for patch frames? do we use minimal diffs or full objects? (tradeoff: complexity vs patch size).
- Should latency_budget_ms be honored strictly at the routing layer (use alternate cheaper model variant) or only at tool-level decisioning?
- How to expose a simple dev-mode that visualizes handshake decisions and simulated latencies for testing?
- UX experiments to validate which placeholder patterns (skeleton, inline text, spinner) minimize user frustration — build A/B harness in SDK.

Immediate next steps (owner: Aisha):
- Prototype minimal server decision logic that respects latency_budget_ms and emits stub frames (tracker: GH-PR-7890).
- Ship web + iOS SDK preview with placeholder template library and instrumentation hooks.
- Create a short playbook for solutions engineers: integration checklist + sample adapters.

Notes to self:
- Keep template library tiny and generic at first. Avoid building a huge schema that we then regret.
- Talk to SRE about how stubs affect billing/quotas (we still count tool invocations when executed normally; for stubs we should surface as "speculated" not billed).

References / links:
